paper_title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate image generation and visual understanding, but are existing single-pathway unlearning methods sufficient to suppress target concepts across both? In this work, we study cross-pathway concept unlearning. Our goal is to prevent a model from both generating images of a target concept and identifying it in input images, while preserving other capabilities. To this end, we introduce UUBench, a diagnostic benchmark covering 30 target concepts and 60 semantically related neighboring concepts. Experiments on representative UMMs show that the evaluated single-pathway methods achieve limited joint forgetting: generation-side editors strongly suppress target generation but yield limited forgetting in visual understanding, while understanding-side baselines struggle to achieve substantial forgetting even in their own pathway. Their direct composition also yields limited joint forgetting. We therefore propose UniForget, achieving joint forgetting rates of 80.0% on BAGEL-7B-MoT and 92.7% on Janus-Pro-7B, outperforming representative baselines. Further analysis reveals trade-offs between joint forgetting and capability preservation.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) increasingly integrate visual understanding and image synthesis within single model, enabling single system to generate high-fidelity images from text while identifying visual entities and answering questions from visual inputs (Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). However, models trained on large web datasets can memorize and reproduce training examples, including personal information (Carlini et al., 2021; 2023). Retraining large models from scratch can be computationally expensive (Maini et al., 2024), and inference-time safeguards may not reliably prevent unwanted outputs (Gandikota et al., 2023). Post-hoc machine unlearning offers an alternative by updating model parameters to reduce the generation or recall of targeted content. To this end, prior efforts have actively explored concept unlearning within isolated single-pathway settings, focusing either on suppressing target concept generation in vision generative models (Gandikota et al., 2023; Kumari et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024) or erasing sensitive factual knowledge from language and multimodal understanding models (Maini et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Recent work has also studied generation-side concept erasure in unified autoregressive models (Fan et al., 2025; Shakibania et al., 2026). However, when generation and understanding are supported by the same unified model, fundamental question arises: are existing single-pathway unlearning methods sufficient to achieve joint forgetting in UMMs? Figure 1 illustrates the joint objective using the Eiffel Tower: suppress target generation and visual identification while preserving non-identity visual information and non-target capabilities. Evaluating both pathways together is therefore necessary to distinguish joint forgetting from localized suppression. *Equal contribution. Work done during internship at ByteDance.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Our empirical investigation shows that shared parameters do not guarantee shared forgetting across pathways. Across the evaluated UMMs, existing unlearning baselines exhibit two primary limitations. First, the evaluated single-pathway methods achieve limited joint forgetting. In our experiments, generation-side adaptations of TIME (Orgad et al., 2023) and UCE (Gandikota et al., 2024) suppress target generation but yield limited forgetting in visual understanding (Section 5.2). Understandingside baselines (Maini et al., 2024) struggle to achieve substantial forgetting even in their own pathway, with modest gains on Janus-Pro-7B and 0.0% TF in generation. Their direct combination also achieves only limited joint forgetting. Second, the evaluated methods often harm other capabilities and neighboring concepts. Instead of genuinely removing the concept, models often resort to refusing questions or giving uninformative responses. Meanwhile, image generation quality drops, and closely related concepts are inadvertently damaged. For example, after erasing the Eiffel Tower, the model may fail to provide informative descriptions of the Tokyo Towers defining features, or mistakenly generate it as generic structure. Therefore, genuine cross-pathway unlearning requires thoroughly eliminating target concepts across both pathways, while strictly preserving generation fidelity, response informativeness, and neighboring knowledge. Figure 1: Illustration of cross-pathway concept unlearning in UMMs. Using the Eiffel Tower as an example, the goal is to suppress target identification in visual understanding and target generation in image synthesis, while preserving non-identity visual information and non-target capabilities. To systematically diagnose these challenges, we introduce UUBENCH, controlled diagnostic evaluation benchmark. UUBENCH includes 30 target concepts across three categories: characters, landmarks, and objects. Each target is paired with two related neighboring concepts, resulting in 90 entities and 720 reference images in total. All data is divided into strictly separated seen and held-out splits. By pairing text-to-image generation and visual question answering tasks around identical entities, UUBENCH evaluates unlearning across both pathways, and checks for damage to neighboring concepts and overall response quality. We also propose UNIFORGET, an unlearning approach that balances generation-side weight editing with understanding-side low-rank updates (Hu et al., 2022). It improves joint forgetting over naive baseline combinations, reaching 80.0% on BAGEL-7B-MoT (Deng et al., 2025) and 92.7% on JanusPro-7B (Chen et al., 2025). Further analysis characterizes the trade-offs between joint forgetting, image quality, and response informativeness. Together, these efforts provide broader and more comprehensive evaluation of cross-pathway unlearning in UMMs. In summary, our contributions are threefold: Cross-Pathway Unlearning Formulation: To the best of our knowledge, we present the first systematic study of joint concept unlearning across image generation and visual understanding in UMMs. Experiments show that evaluated single-pathway methods achieve limited joint forgetting. Diagnostic Benchmark (UUBENCH): We construct UUBENCH, controlled diagnostic benchmark spanning 30 target and 60 neighboring concepts, establishing paired generation-understanding tasks and joint metrics to assess unlearning efficacy, specificity, and capability preservation. Unlearning Method and Empirical Analysis: We propose UNIFORGET, an unlearning approach that balances generation-side weight editing with understanding-side low-rank updates, outperforming the combined baseline. We further examine the effects of editing on both pathways and reveal trade-offs between joint forgetting and capability preservation.

sections.title: 2 CROSS-PATHWAY CONCEPT UNLEARNING
sections.content: We study how UMMs can unlearn target concept in both image generation and visual understanding within the same model, while preserving their other capabilities.

sections.title: 2.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION AND CORE DISTINCTIONS
sections.content: Let Mθ denote UMM supporting text-to-image generation Tgen and image-to-text understanding Tund, where θ includes both shared and task-specific parameters. Given target concept c, an unlearning intervention updates the model parameters to an edited checkpoint θ. To evaluate unlearning across the two pathways, we make the following distinctions: Pathway-specific forgetting. Forgetting is assessed independently in each pathway. Under Tgen, generated images should not contain recognizable depictions of c. Under Tund, responses to identity queries about target images should omit the target name and aliases while providing accurate category-level descriptions, rather than refusing, giving irrelevant answers, or assigning an incorrect alternative identity. Success in one pathway does not imply success in the other. Joint forgetting. We assess whether θ simultaneously satisfies the forgetting criteria in both pathways for c. This serves as an outcome-level baseline indicating that target identity is suppressed across both modalities, regardless of whether it arises from transfer or joint optimization. Utility-preserving joint forgetting. We assess the extent to which joint forgetting is achieved while preserving (i) generation quality and non-target prompt fidelity, (ii) informative visual descriptions of target images, and (iii) performance on neighboring concepts and general tasks. For each target c, we evaluate both pathways using generation prompts and held-out target images. The pairing procedure, forgetting criteria, and utility metrics are described in Section 3.2.

sections.title: 3 UUBENCH: A CROSS-PATHWAY DIAGNOSTIC BENCHMARK
sections.content: Motivated by these distinctions, we introduce UUBENCH, controlled diagnostic benchmark for evaluating concept forgetting and utility preservation across image generation and visual understanding. Figure 2 summarizes its concept categories, paired tasks, and evaluation metrics.

sections.title: 3.1 DATASET AND TASK CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Target concepts and neighbors. UUBENCH includes 30 target concepts across three categories: characters, landmarks, and generic objects (10 per category). Each target is paired with two distinct, same-category neighbors sharing visual or functional attributes (e.g., Eiffel Tower paired with Tokyo Tower & Blackpool Tower). We use these 60 neighbors to assess the preservation of non-target generation and understanding capabilities. In total, the benchmark contains 90 concepts. Reference images and data splits. Reference images were collected from publicly accessible media repositories and manually reviewed for concept identity and visual clarity. Each concept has eight images: three for understanding-side edit calibration and supervision, five held out for evaluation, totaling 720 images. Editing and evaluation use strictly disjoint template groups for both image generation and visual understanding to prevent prompt memorization. Paired task construction. For each target and its two neighbors, we construct generation and understanding tasks evaluated using the same edited checkpoint. Generation prompts specify the concept name, e.g., Generate realistic image of Eiffel Tower. Understanding inputs pair held-out reference images with two types of questions: identity questions ask the model to name the subject, whereas non-identity questions ask about its appearance, context or request an open-ended visual description. Template examples and question counts are provided in Appendix A.1.

(3) Does joint unlearning compromise visual utility, image quality, and neighboring concepts? We conduct our experiments on UUBENCH following the standard settings described in Section 3. To evaluate UNIFORGET across different UMM architectures, we select two widely used UMMs with distinct architectural designs as our base models. Specifically, BAGEL-7B-MoT (Deng et al., 2025) represents the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture (Liang et al., 2024), which employs modality-specific Transformer parameters for multimodal processing. In contrast, Janus-Pro7B (Chen et al., 2025) adopts shared unified Transformer backbone while decoupling the visual encoding pathways for multimodal understanding and image generation. To comprehensively evaluate UNIFORGET, we compare it against three categories of baselines: (1) Generation-oriented editing methods, including UCE (Gandikota et al., 2024) and TIME (Orgad et al., 2023). (2) Understanding-oriented unlearning methods, including gradient descent (GD) and KL-based optimization (KL) (Maini et al., 2024). (3) TIME + GD, compositional baseline that directly combines generation-side TIME with understanding-side GD in the same checkpoint.

sections.title: 5.2 MAIN RESULTS AND KEY FINDINGS
sections.content: We report the main results in Table 2, and organize key findings as follows: Finding 1: Single-pathway baselines achieve limited joint forgetting. Generation-side editors effectively suppress target concepts in synthesis, but achieve limited forgetting in visual understanding. For example, TIME achieves 100.0% TF on BAGEL-7B-MoT and 96.7% on Janus-Pro-7B, yet yields only 24.0% and 30.7% DF, respectively. The evaluated understanding-side baselines struggle to achieve substantial forgetting even within their own pathway, with only modest gains on Janus-Pro-7B. Neither GD nor KL produces generation-side forgetting, with 0.0% TF on both backbones. Together, these results show that the evaluated single-pathway methods remain insufficient for joint unlearning. Finding 2: Coordinated pathway-specific editing improves over naive composition. Directly combining TIME and GD, the strongest generation-side and understanding-side baselines, achieves only 31.3% Unified Forget on BAGEL-7B-MoT and 41.3% on Janus-Pro-7B. In contrast, UNIFORGET reaches 80.0% and 92.7%, while achieving 100.0% TF on both backbones. Unified Strict Forget also improves by 18.9 and 27.0 percentage points, respectively, showing that UNIFORGET outperforms direct composition even when image quality and visual utility are considered. These results support coordinating pathway-specific updates rather than simply combining existing methods. Finding 3: Joint forgetting and capability preservation exhibit distinct trade-offs. Under utilityaware evaluation, UNIFORGET achieves Unified Strict Forget rates of 47.6% on BAGEL-7B-MoT and 58.0% on Janus-Pro-7B, showing that target concepts could be suppressed while retaining useful capabilities. Janus performs better on both joint metrics, whereas BAGEL better preserves generation capabilities for neighboring concepts, achieving an SR rate of 84.6%, compared with 73.2% for Janus. These findings also reflect the necessity of evaluating forgetting and capability preservation together.

sections.title: 5.3 GENERAL CAPABILITY PRESERVATION
sections.content: To assess whether the concept-local effects measured by UUBENCH coincide with broad capability changes, we evaluate the selected checkpoints on standard generation and visual-understanding benchmarks. General visual understanding is comparatively stable on MMBench and MME-P. Relative to the base models, UNIFORGET changes MMBench from 88.4% to 87.8% and MME-P from 83.3% to 82.1% on BAGEL-7B-MoT; on Janus-Pro-7B, the corresponding scores change from 79.1% to 77.2% and from 76.8% to 76.1%. The main exception is BAGELs MME-C score, which decreases from 85.5% to 77.7%, whereas Janus remains nearly unchanged (35.0% to 34.6%). On the generation side, GenEval decreases from 72.7% to 63.4% on BAGEL and from 78.9% to 70.1% on Janus, while DPG-Bench changes from 83.4% to 79.9% and from 83.1% to 74.2%, respectively. This asymmetry suggests that generation capabilities may be more vulnerable during cross-pathway unlearning. Complete results are reported in Table 3 of Appendix C.1.

sections.title: 6 ANALYSIS OF JOINT FORGETTING AND CAPABILITY PRESERVATION
sections.content: To better understand the results in Table 2, we conduct component ablations and examine composition strength, multi-concept scaling, and robustness to perturbations.

sections.title: 6.1 COMPONENT ABLATIONS AND SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
sections.content: Table 4 compares the Full generation configuration with three variants: Last-token, Single-template, and Neighbors-only. Compared with Neighbors-only, Full maintains 100.0% TF on both models while improving NR from 90.4% to 98.1% on BAGEL and from 85.7% to 92.9% on Janus. Thus, the full construction improves neighbor preservation while maintaining target forgetting. Table 5 reports cumulative understanding-side ablations. Starting with Positive-only LoRA, we successively add Pairwise preference, Masked KL, and Anti-collapse, retaining all previous objectives at each step. On BAGEL, extending the configuration that includes Pairwise preference with Masked KL improves DF from 77.2% to 80.0% and TU from 63.8% to 72.2%. On Janus, further extending the cumulative configuration that includes Masked KL with Anti-collapse maintains DF at 92.7% while improving TU from 67.1% to 75.6%. These comparisons show how specific components help balance forgetting and visual utility. Further details are provided in Appendix C.2.

sections.title: 6.2 COMPOSITION STRENGTH AND THE FORGETTING–PRESERVATION TRADE-OFF
sections.content: Figure 3 examines how the understanding update strength ρ affects target forgetting and visual utility when applied to the generation-edited model. We also introduce Collapse, defined as the rate of degenerate responses, to distinguish target forgetting from general failure to produce meaningful answers. Together, these metrics capture both the forgetting gains and the response qualities. On BAGEL-7B-MoT, increasing ρ from the selected value of 0.4 to 0.6 improves DF from 80.0% to 93.3%, but lowers TU from 72.2% to 55.6%. On Janus-Pro-7B, increasing ρ from the selected value of 1.0 to 1.2 brings little improvement in DF (92.7% to 93.3%), while TU falls from 75.6% to 55.0%. These results show that stronger understanding updates improve target forgetting at the cost of visual utility, with different trade-offs across the two models.

sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Concept erasure and editing in generative models. Concept erasure has been studied extensively in text-to-image diffusion models (Kumari et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2024). ESD fine-tunes the denoising network to suppress target concepts (Gandikota et al., 2023). TIME uses closed-form updates to edit implicit visual associations, while UCE supports concept erasure and editing with an explicit preservation objective (Orgad et al., 2023; Gandikota et al., 2024). MACE further studies multi-concept erasure in diffusion models while evaluating non-target specificity (Lu et al., 2024). UnlearnCanvas evaluates forgetting, non-target retention, and image quality, and includes tests of adversarial prompts and sequential unlearning (Zhang et al., 2024). Other work examines the reversibility of concept erasure through further fine-tuning (Liu & Zhang, 2025). These studies mainly evaluate unlearning through generated images, while we assess whether the same target is suppressed in both generation and visual understanding within unified model. Multimodal unlearning and evaluation. TOFU and MUSE evaluate both target forgetting and the preservation of non-target knowledge in language models (Maini et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). For multimodal models, MLLMU-Bench and CLEAR evaluate target recall under text-only and imageconditioned queries, together with retained capabilities (Liu et al., 2025; Dontsov et al., 2025). SIU and MMUnlearner study visual recognition unlearning while preserving textual factual knowledge about the same targets (Li et al., 2024; Huo et al., 2025). SIU also measures response fluency and diversity (Li et al., 2024). Recent studies, including UMU-Bench and UNLINK-VL, further examine forgetting across text-only and image-conditioned inputs (Wen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). These multimodal studies mainly assess unlearning through textual responses, rather than jointly assessing target suppression in image generation and visual understanding. UMMs and concept unlearning. Chameleon, Show-o, Janus-Pro, and BAGEL support both visual understanding and image generation through different architectural designs (Chameleon Team, 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025). Previously, EAR performs generation-side concept erasure in Janus-Pro-7B by updating its language-model backbone (Fan et al., 2025), while Obliviate further reports multi-concept erasure and general visual-understanding utility (Shakibania et al., 2026). However, these studies primarily focus on generation-side of the unified model, while we jointly evaluate forgetting across both pathways.

sections.title: 8 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: This study has several limitations. Experiments cover two 7B UMMs and 30 target concepts, leaving generalization to larger models and broader domains for future work. Image quality and visual utility are assessed using automated metrics and LLM judges, which may differ from human judgment. The evaluation focuses on behavioral forgetting under standard prompts, while certified information deletion from model weights remains beyond its scope.

sections.title: 9 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we investigate cross-pathway concept unlearning in UMMs and introduce UUBENCH, controlled diagnostic benchmark covering unlearning for both generation and visual understanding. Our experiments show that the evaluated single-pathway methods and their direct composition achieve limited joint forgetting. Generation-side editing strongly suppresses target generation but yields limited forgetting in visual understanding, while understanding-side baselines struggle to achieve substantial forgetting even within their own pathway. In contrast, our method UNIFORGET improves joint forgetting while preserving utility. However, scaling to multiple concepts and maintaining robustness to adversarial inputs remain challenging. We hope UUBENCH provides rigorous evaluation foundation and encourages future research into robust, unified multimodal unlearning.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work investigates concept unlearning in UMMs to mitigate the risks of generating or recognizing sensitive, proprietary, or copyrighted visual concepts. The benchmarks and models studied in this work use publicly available resources and established research checkpoints. The evaluation procedures are designed to benchmark privacy, safety, and alignment compliance without generating harmful, discriminatory, or offensive content. All empirical results adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To ensure the full reproducibility of our empirical findings, we provide comprehensive specifications of the UUBENCH dataset, model architectures, training procedures, objective functions, automated judge prompts, and hyperparameters in Appendices A, B, and E. The source code and benchmark evaluation will be released publicly upon publication.

sections.content: A.1 BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION DETAILS The reference-image bank covers characters, landmarks, and objects, with 30 target concepts (10 per category) and 60 neighboring concepts (20 per category), totaling 90 entities. Each entity has 3 seen and 5 held-out images. Targets contribute 90 seen and 150 held-out images (240 total), while neighbors contribute 180 seen and 300 held-out images (480 total). It contains 720 images in total. Registry and curation. Each concept has canonical name, registered aliases and surface variants, generic category, and fixed replacement phrase. For each target, we select two same-category neighbors with related appearance or function but distinct identities. Before constructing task-specific records, the data compiler validates concept identities, image paths, split membership, and provenance hashes. Candidate images that fail manual review or have unresolved issues are excluded from the active reference set. Split and template isolation. For each entity, image indices 02 are seen and indices 37 are held out. Understanding edits use only seen target and neighbor images. sections.title: B IMPLEMENTATION AND REPRODUCIBILITY
sections.content: We report the implementation settings, training configurations, and compute environment. We use random seed 42 for all experiments. All quantitative results in the main text and appendices are reported as the mean of three repeated measurements. B.1 AUTOMATED JUDGE SPECIFICATIONS Automatic evaluations use gpt-5.4-mini through the OpenAI Responses API. Each query uses maximum output budget of 2048 tokens, reasoning.effort="high", temperature=1.0, and top_p=1.0. Input images are converted to RGB, resized to maximum dimension of 1024 pixels, and encoded as JPEG with quality 90. The understanding judge receives the reference image, question, evaluation track/type, before/after answers, structured JSON schema, and concept names and aliases as evaluation metadata. The evaluated model receives the standard category-worded questions. The judge returns separate labels for explicit naming leakage, visual correctness, identity and generic-category correctness, specificity and hallucinations. The generation judge uses separate rubric to compare original and edited images. B.2 GENERATION EDITING AND SYNTHESIS Closed-form regression edits the k_proj and v_proj projection matrices within the language models self-attention blocks (0-indexed layers 027 for BAGEL-7B-MoT, yielding 56 matrices; layers 029 for Janus-Pro-7B, yielding 60 matrices). Separate cross-attention modules remain unchanged. Category-generic textual anchor compilation. At data-compilation time, each target inherits one fixed textual phrase from its registered category: generic landmark, generic fictional character, or generic object. All targets in category share its fixed textual anchor. Calibration templates include photo of {N} and {N} against the sky. UNIFORGET instantiates all 20 templates once with the target name and once with its category-generic textual anchor, producing 20 paired target/anchor prompts under whole-prompt pooling. The target states remain separate columns of Ke. The corresponding anchor prompts are passed through the pre-edit projection ; their 20 outputs are averaged to va and the same vector is tiled across columns to form Ve = va1. The preservation bank contains 98 prompts: 9 generic prompts, 29 non-target concept prompts, and 60 neighbor prompts. Their states form Kp and their original outputs form Vp = Kp. Registered neighbors provide preservation constraints, while the category-generic phrases serve as redirection anchors. Both the ridge coefficient λ and preservation weight γ are 1.0. This 20-template bank is specific to UNIFORGET. Editing and evaluation use disjoint template groups for both generation and understanding. For image synthesis, Base and Edited checkpoints use matched random seed 42 per prompt, with seeds reset prior to each sample generation. BAGEL-7B-MoT synthesizes 512 512 images using 50 diffusion steps, timestep shift 3.0, text CFG 4.0, image CFG 1.0, active CFG interval [0.4, 1.0], and global renormalization (cfg_renorm_min=1.0). Janus-Pro-7B autoregressively generates 576 discrete image tokens at 384 384 resolution using CFG 5.0 and temperature 1.0. Generation edits apply at full intensity (α = 1.0). B.3 UNDERSTANDING TRAINING AND INFERENCE Understanding fine-tuning starts from the generation-edited checkpoint, freezes its backbone, and trains low-rank adapters (LoRA) with rank = 8, scaling α = 16, and dropout 0 on the k_proj and v_proj projections of layers 12, 16, and 20. sections.title: D MATCHED QUALITATIVE EXAMPLES
sections.content: We present paired qualitative results from Base and UNIFORGET. Colosseum and Batman illustrate target suppression and retained visual description. Astronomical Telescope presents limitation case: target-name suppression is accompanied by loss of visual detail in the understanding responses. Both backbones use the same target prompts and paired neighbor prompts. All generation images use random seed 42, and Base and edited outputs are shown side by side. Understanding comparisons use the same held-out image and the same identity and visible-attribute questions. We pair stored Base answers with freshly generated UNIFORGET answers using greedy decoding. Images are presented as provided in the source data. These examples illustrate changes in model behavior after editing. The full source package covers five concepts, including Darth Vader and Eiffel Tower, with 40 generation images, five shared input images, and 80 answers covering four question types.
